The program reads a number of students \(N\) and a number of friendship pairs \(M\). 
For every pair \((x,y)\) it puts \(y\) into a set that belongs to \(x\) and \(x\) into the set that belongs to \(y\). 
Thus each student has a set that contains all of his friends – this is the graph representation.

An array `d` of length \(N+1\) is created. 
All entries except `d[1]` are set to a very large value (`INF`). 
`d[i]` will later hold the number of “steps” needed for student \(i\) to learn the news.

A queue is created and the first student (id 1) is put into it. 
While the queue is not empty the program removes the front element `u`. 
For every friend `v` of `u` (obtained by iterating over the set `G[u]`) it checks whether `d[v]` is still `INF`. 
If it is, that means student `v` has not yet learned the news, so the program sets `d[v] = d[u] + 1` and pushes `v` onto the back of the queue. 
The value `d[v]` is therefore one more than the value of the student that just informed it, representing the time step when `v` receives the news.

Because the queue is processed in a first‑in, first‑out order, all students that learn the news at the same step are processed consecutively before any student that learns it later. 
The queue guarantees that a student is examined only after all students that could inform it earlier have already been examined.

After the queue becomes empty, every student has a finite `d` value. 
The program scans all `d[i]` and keeps the maximum value in `sol`. 
This maximum is the largest number of steps needed for any student to learn the news, i.e., the moment when the last student receives it. 
Finally it prints `sol`.

The list is stored as a vector of vectors: each inner vector contains the indices of neighbours.

The program then starts a process from student 0 (the teacher, id 1 in the input). 
A queue `q` is used to keep the students that need to be processed. 
An array `dist` of length `n` stores how many time steps it takes for each student to learn the news; it is initialized with a very large number (`1e9`) to mean “not yet reached”. 
`dist[0]` is set to `0` because the teacher knows the news at time 0, and student 0 is pushed into the queue.

While the queue is not empty, the program removes the front element `u`. 
For every neighbour `v` of `u` (obtained from `g[u]`), it checks whether `dist[v]` is still the large initial value. 
If so, this neighbour has not learned the news yet. The program sets `dist[v]` to `dist[u] + 1` (one more time step than `u`), and pushes `v` onto the back of the queue. 
Thus neighbours are processed in the order they are discovered: first all students that learn the news one step after the current one, then those that learn it two steps later, and so on.

The queue guarantees that students are processed level by level: all students that learn the news at the same time are removed from the queue before any student that learns it later. 
No separate counter for the current time step is kept; the time is stored directly in `dist`.

After the queue becomes empty, every student has a finite distance value. 
The program finds the largest value in `dist` using `max_element`. 
This largest value is the number of time steps needed for the last student to learn the news, and it is printed as the result.
